302	
303	Both read and change nothing. In cost and storage runs, `print` and
304	`observe.raw` are the state `absys FILE` prints at the end of the text of
305	stages 1 to *k* (with `--each` in a stage that spawns, the state after
306	each assertion, from which each computation's is read).
307	
308	### 3.9 The constants block
309	
310	Every constant of every stage is in **one block in the prelude**, between
311	a comment line containing `CONSTANTS BEGIN` and one containing
312	`CONSTANTS END`. The block is a **table, never given to the system**: one
313	constant per line, `NAME = VALUE`, the value on that line (comment lines
314	and blank lines are allowed; a `%` ends the value):
315	
316	    % CONSTANTS BEGIN
317	    c1 = 41
318	    c2 = 'red'
319	    facts = [[1, 'a'], [2, 'b']]
320	    % CONSTANTS END
321	
322	The program's text refers to the constants by name (`pr = [c1, d]`).
323	**When the harness gives a section to the system, it replaces each name
324	of the table, in that section's text, by its value**, so that what the
325	system receives is `pr = [41, d]`. A constant therefore reaches the system
326	only with the section that uses it: a constant of stage 3 is not in the
327	system, as information or as a name, before stage 3 is posed (no
328	anticipation, `PROTOCOL.md`, "Writing a program", rule 5). A name used in
329	the prelude (in a definition) is given with the prelude, at stage 1.
330	
331	What is replaced, exactly: an identifier (the system's: a letter or `_`,
332	then letters, digits and `_`, and, after a small letter, `-` between
333	letters, as in `math-course`) equal to a name of the table. Nothing is
334	replaced inside a quoted constant (`'…'`, `"…"`), inside a comment, or in
335	a name written with a prime (1969: a new local name). The value is put in
336	as written in the table, with no change. So:
337	
338	- name constants with identifiers that the program uses for nothing else;
339	- a constant used inside a lambda is replaced like any other (the value,
340	  not the name, reaches the system, so the scoping rules of 3.3 do not
341	  arise).
342	
343	The verifier replaces only the lines between the markers. The harness
344	records `constants.how: "block"` when the markers are present, else
345	`"none"`. `check` parses each section after the replacement, as the
346	system will receive it, and reports a line of the block that is not
347	`NAME = VALUE`. Absys reads no input, so there is no `input` form.
348	
349	### 3.10 Effects (P11): emit
350	
351	The harness's `emit(m)` is written, in Absys,
352	
353	    tout("emit", M)
354	
355	with the term to emit as its second argument. `tout` is the system's own
356	output assertion (Elcock 1990, note 11): it waits until its term has no
357	uninstantiated variable, and then performs one output, `emit = VALUE`, in
358	the derivation it is in. In P11 runs the harness switches the system's
359	trace on (`.trace`, or `--trace`), and every `output` event of the trace
360	whose text begins `emit = ` becomes one entry of the log, `entry` being
361	the rest of it, the system's rendering of the term (`'red'`, `[1,2]`), in
362	the order the trace shows them. An output performed in a derivation that
363	later fails stays in the log: nothing the system does removes an entry.
364	Entries made while a reposed run replays an earlier stage carry
365	`during_replay_of`. Behaviour runs write to
366	`OUTDIR/<instance>.effects.jsonl`; the separate run that measures a
367	restart cost, and every cost and storage run, write to
368	`OUTDIR/<instance>.effects-observation.jsonl`. Neither is ever reset.
369	
370	**Commit stages** (P11c stage 3, P11d stage 2): Absys keeps every
371	derivation live and selects none. The section may be empty (comments
372	only). `answers(1)` reports the first derivation printed, as for any
373	any-one query; no commitment is recorded, and none is replayed when a
374	later stage is reposed (QUESTIONS, A6).
375	
376	### 3.11 Provenance
377	
378	At the top of the file, in comments, the lines `% AUTHOR: …`,
379	`% PRECURSOR-SEEN: yes|no` (whether its author had seen the E01–E09
380	programs) and `% IDIOM: …` (the source of each idiom). `check` warns if
381	there is no `AUTHOR` line.
382	
383	### 3.12 H tokens
384	
385	`METRICS.md`, class H: the harness's own calls as they appear in a
386	program. In an Absys program they are:
387	
388	| construct | H tokens |
389	|---|---|
390	| the emit stub's binding, `tout("emit", T)` | `tout`, `(`, `"emit"`, `,` and `)`; the term `T` is classed on its own (rule 10) |
391	
392	Nothing else in a program is H. The markers are comments; the parameter
393	assertions are written by the harness, not the program; answers are
394	collected from what the system prints by itself, with no call in the
395	program, so there is no output adapter. A program's uses of a parameter's
396	name (`n`), its constants block and its definitions are classed by the
397	rules of `METRICS.md`.
398	
399	### 3.13 A complete minimal example
400	
401	A made-up problem, not one of P01–P16 (`qualification/stages-qualification.json`, X10):
402	
403	> **X10a.** `pair(A, B, P)` holds when P is the list `[A, B]`.
404	> Stage 1: `pair(a, b, pr)`. Stage 2: `pr = [⟨k⟩, d]`. Stage 3: `d = ⟨atom⟩`.
405	> Unknowns a, b, pr, d. Constants: ⟨k⟩ = 41, ⟨atom⟩ = `'red'`.
406	
407	The program, `qualification/programs/x10-pair.abs`:
408	
409	```
410	% AUTHOR: harness-absys (an agent), for the harness's qualification. MADE UP: not a problem program.
411	% PRECURSOR-SEEN: no. IDIOM: a lambda procedure, as in Elcock 1990 p. 8.
412	% CONSTANTS BEGIN
413	c1 = 41
414	c2 = 'red'
415	% CONSTANTS END
416	pair = lambda A, B, P {P = [A, B]}
417	% STAGE 1
418	pair(a, b, pr)
419	% STAGE 2
420	pr = [c1, d]
421	% STAGE 3
422	d = c2
423	```
424	
425	What the system receives, in one session, and what the harness collects
426	(from the qualification's behaviour record):
427	
428	| stage | written to the repl | `answers(20)`: the one derivation | state |
429	|---|---|---|---|
430	| 1 | the prelude without the block (lines 1, 2 and 7), `.help`, `% STAGE 1` and `pair(a, b, pr)`, `.help`, then `?` and `? a`, `? b`, `? pr`, `? d` | `a  uninstantiated`, `b  uninstantiated`, `pr = [a,b]` | finished |
431	| 2 | `% STAGE 2`, `pr = [41, d]`, `.help`, `?`, … | `a = 41`, `b = d   (suspended: b = d)`, `pr = [41,b]`, `suspended   b = d` | suspended |
432	| 3 | `% STAGE 3`, `d = 'red'`, `.help`, `?`, … | `a = 41`, `b = 'red'`, `pr = [41,'red']`, `d = 'red'` | finished |
433	
434	41 is not in the system before stage 2, nor `'red'` before stage 3.
435	
436	Its H tokens: none. Snippets for the other forms are in
437	`qualification/programs/`: SPAWN (`x17-spawn.abs`), PART with a parameter
438	(`x19-parts.abs`), emit (`x18-emit.abs`), the 1969 notation
439	(`x20-arith.ab1`).
440	
441	## 4. Modes
442	
443	| mode | process | what is of record |
444	|---|---|---|
445	| behaviour | one `absys-measure repl --full` for the run (a new one only to repose) | answers, `observe`, `print`, execution state, the effects log. No step count: the repl reports none |
446	| cost | per stage, `absys-measure FILE --measure --full` on stages 1..k; `--trace` too where the budget is 10⁶ | `steps.stage` (the steps of stage k's assertions: the incremental cost), `steps.restated` (all of the run), `restart_cost` (stages 1..k−1, in-run), `to_end`, `repeated_work` |
447	| storage | the same command, with `--trace` only in P11 | the store vector, `alternatives.peak` (derivations, exact), the state's suspended processes |
448	
449	- **Steps** are the system's (one step of the machine, as `--steps`
450	  counts them), read only from `--measure`'s table, the systems file's
451	  qualified measurement. Sampling the store adds time, not steps
452	  (systems file). Cost and storage records both keep what `--measure`
453	  gave; the figure of record is the mode's. Behaviour records have
454	  `steps.stage: null`.
455	- **Store** (`store.quantities`): the ten quantities of `--measure`, each
456	  with `boundary` (after the stage's last assertion) and `peak` (the
457	  largest value after any step of the stage's assertions, or when each
458	  was added), `kind: "exact"` (exact at the granularity of steps). A stage
459	  with no assertion has the boundary of the last assertion before it and
460	  no peak.
461	- **Suspended work** (`suspended`) is what the system prints as suspended,
462	  in every mode, counted by kind under `--measure`'s names
463	  (`susp_equations` for an equation between unknowns, `susp_applications`
464	  for "waits for a definition" or "for its key", `susp_relations` for
465	  "waits for two of its numbers" or "for its term", `susp_negations` for
466	  "waits for its variables" or "cannot be decided yet"), summed over
467	  derivations. The printer shows only processes still waiting on an
468	  uninstantiated variable; `--measure`'s `susp_*` in the store also count
469	  equations and arithmetic relations that stay associated with their
470	  variables after every one is bound (`docs/decisions.md`, rule 10), so
471	  the two may differ.
472	- **Repeated work** (cost mode, budget 10⁶): `reactivating_events`, the
473	  number of trace events of the stage's assertions that reactivated
474	  suspended processes (`… reactivated …`: a variable was bound and the
475	  processes waiting on it went back to the goal). Not measured (`null`)
476	  where the budget is 10⁸, whose traces would be too large to keep.
477	- **P13**: `cpu_time_s` and `max_rss_kb` of the behaviour run's process
478	  (`getrusage` through `os.wait4`), for growth only.
479	
480	## 5. Budget, safety limit, reposing
481	
482	- **Budget.** `--steps B`, B the problem's budget, is the system's own
483	  budget, and it counts **per assertion**: each assertion is elaborated
484	  for at most B steps. A stage of several assertions can therefore spend
485	  more than B in all before the system reports budget (QUESTIONS, A1);
486	  cost records say so in a note when it happens. A stage is *budget* when
487	  the system's state reports derivations "still elaborating when the
488	  budget ran out".
489	- **Continuing after budget: yes, in every configuration.** The derivations
490	  still elaborating stay in the session, and the next assertion accepted
491	  goes on elaborating them, with a new budget. So after *budget* the next
492	  stage is posed into the same session, `continued_after_budget: true`.
493	- **Safety limit.** For an incremental stage, from writing its first line
494	  to reading the last reply; for a reposed one, the whole run, replay
495	  included. When it is reached the harness sends **SIGKILL** to the
496	  system's process (`safety_limit.how_stopped`), records what it had read,
497	  and, where the problem allows, reruns the stage once with the raised
498	  limit, by reposing (the session is gone). P12, P13 and P16: no rerun.
499	- **Reposing** (after *error*, after a final *timeout*, a safety rerun):
500	  a new session, into which the harness writes the parameters, the
501	  prelude and every section of stages 1 to *k*−1 in order, each followed
502	  by `.help`, replacements and withdrawals included, then stage *k* as
503	  usual. The repl gives no step count, so the restart cost is measured on
504	  a **separate run** of that same text with `absys-measure json`, which
505	  reports each assertion's steps (the same count as `--measure`'s, as the
506	  qualification shows) without sampling the store
507	  (`restart_cost_method: "separate-run"`). It stops at a syntax error,
508	  where the repl goes on, so after an error it may undercount, and the
509	  record says so in `harness_faults`.
510	- **Error.** The repl reports a syntax or static error and goes on; the
511	  harness records the stage as *error* with the message verbatim, and
512	  poses the next stage by reposing, as `PROTOCOL.md` says. A system
513	  process that ends on its own (a crash, or killed by the kernel) is
514	  *error* too, with its exit status or signal.
515	- **When a reposed stage's replay itself cannot finish** (the replay is
516	  killed for lack of memory), no restart cost can be measured, and the
517	  record does not validate: it is kept as `.INVALID.json`, exit 3
518	  (QUESTIONS, A12).
519	
520	## 6. `check`
521	
522	    harnesses/absys/check CONFIGURATION PROGRAM
523	
524	Absys has no parse-only mode. `absys lsp` cannot serve: its diagnostics
525	*run* the text (`src/lsp.rs`, `analyse`, with a budget of 20 000 steps).
526	So `check` does this, the same for every configuration (the flags change
527	nothing a parser sees):
528	
529	1. It reads the program's bytes and finds its sections, as `run` does
530	   (3.1); it reports misplaced markers, numbering, and a missing `AUTHOR`
531	   line (a warning).
532	2. For each section, as the harness would give it, it does what the repl
533	   does line by line (3.2): after each line, it gives the text read since
534	   the last complete assertion to `absys-measure json FILE --steps 0`.
535	   That command parses the text and compiles each assertion and adds it
536	   to the goal, with **a budget of zero steps**: no step of the machine
537	   is taken, so no equation, application, `or`, `not`, `set` or `tout` is
538	   elaborated. `check` reads only the error (with its line and column)
539	   and the number of assertions, and stops if the system reports any step
540	   or event at all.
541	3. It prints each error verbatim, with its line in the program, each line
542	   that the repl would take as a command, and each section that ends in
543	   an unfinished assertion. Exit 0 when there is none, 1 otherwise.
544	
545	It never prints anything the program would compute. The qualification
546	shows it on a program whose only effect, run, is to output a marker: the
547	marker is not in `check`'s output, while running the program prints it.
548	Absys has no means of writing a file, so no file test is possible.
549	
550	## 7. Confounds
551	
552	Everything the harness does beyond passing stages in, collecting answers
553	through the system's mechanism and reading state (copied into every
554	record's `run.confounds`):
555	
556	1. Behaviour runs use the measurement build with `--full` (printer only),
557	   not the baseline build (2).
558	2. The `.help` line after each section, to know where the system's output
559	   for it ends; a section ending inside an unfinished assertion turns it
560	   into a syntax error (3.2).
561	3. `?` and `? NAME` to read the state (3.8).
562	4. The parameters' assertions, written by the harness (3.4).
563	5. PART sections chosen by the instance's order (3.5).
564	6. Spawned computations accepted one after another into the one session,
565	   each read right after its section (3.6).
566	7. The budget is per assertion (5).
567	8. Cost and storage runs are a new process per stage, on stages 1..k (3.2).
568	9. The restart cost of a reposed behaviour stage is measured on a separate
569	   `json` run (5).
570	10. The trace is switched on in P11 runs and in cost runs with the 10⁶
571	    budget (3.10, 4).
572	11. `answers(cap)` takes the first `cap` derivations of the printed state (3.7).
573	12. Each constant's name is replaced by its value in the section that uses
574	    it, when that section is given; the block itself is never given (3.9).
575	
576	## 8. Qualification
577	
578	`qualification/run-qualification` reruns everything; its output is
579	`qualification/output.txt`, and its records are in
580	`qualification/records/`. See [`qualification/README.md`](qualification/README.md).

# Absys programs: batch 1A (P01, P02, P03)

*Phase 5 (`PROTOCOL.md`, "Implementation"), wave 1. Written against
`spec-1.0.1` and the contract of `harnesses/absys/README.md`. No program
here has been run. Only `harnesses/absys/check` was used, and it reports
no errors for any of them, in each configuration.*

**Author of every program:** `implementation-absys`, an agent (Claude
Opus 5.5, model id `claude-opus-5-5`), with its own context. It had not
seen any earlier work on this study.

**Precursor programs (E01–E09): not seen.** None of their texts was read.
`/opt/src/absys/research/`, `/opt/src/absys-measure/research/` and
`/opt/src/absys/docs/research.md` were not opened. Two things that bear on
these problems were seen in the documentation the brief allows, and are
disclosed:

- the reconstruction's `README.md` summarises findings of E02, E03, E06,
  E07 and E09 in prose. It gives, among others, the result of
  `app([1,2], S, T)` (close to P01b) and of `x + y = 10`, `x - y = 4`;
- the tutorial (ch. 8) and `examples/relation-list.ab2` give Elcock's own
  1982 text `u+v = 16 and w*u = v and u+10 = 12` with its trace. P02 is
  taken from that published source. It is a source, not a precursor
  program.

## Layout

One file per sub-problem, `programs/absys/<configuration>/<sub-problem>.ab1`,
for the three configurations of `systems/absys/README.md`:

    programs/absys/absys/              P01a P01b P01c P02a P02b P02c P03a P03b P03c P03d P03e P03f
    programs/absys/absys-depth-first/  the same twelve, byte for byte
    programs/absys/absys-wake-back/    the same twelve, byte for byte

**The three configurations share one text** for every sub-problem. The
flags (`--search depth-first`, `--wake back`) change how the machine
schedules derivations and returned relations, not the language, so the
natural program is the same text in each. The copies are identical; each
configuration has its own path only because the harness takes one.

P02b is one file for its six instances: its relations are PART sections
`R1`, `R2`, `R3`, and the harness gives part `order[k-1]` at stage *k*
(`harnesses/absys/README.md`, 3.5). Every other sub-problem has one
instance and uses STAGE sections.

## Notation

`systems/absys/README.md`, Notation: the earliest notation that has every
construct the problem needs. All twelve are in the **1969 notation**
(`.ab1`, Absys 1):

- P02 needs arithmetic, which the reconstruction has in the 1969 notation
  only (`docs/decisions.md`, rule 23).
- P01 and P03 need equations, lists, and a relation defined with
  alternatives. The 1969 notation has all three (`lambda … begin {A or B}
  end`, `[a;b]`, `[h&t]`), so it is the earliest, and the 1990 notation of
  Elcock's `app` is not used. The relations are written as relations (no
  `=> z` result, no `key`).

## Per configuration and sub-problem

The same entries hold for `absys`, `absys-depth-first` and
`absys-wake-back`.

| sub-problem | program | primary or variant | expressibility, as the author sees it | S used |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P01a | `P01a.ab1`: `x = y`; `y = z`; `z = zval` | primary | expressible | none |
| P01b | `P01b.ab1`: conc; `conc(left, s, t)`; `s = sval` | primary | expressible | none |
| P01c | `P01c.ab1`: `x = [pfx&x]` | primary | expressible (no occur check, `docs/decisions.md` rule 8) | none |
| P02a | `P02a.ab1`: R1, R2, R3, one per stage | primary | expressible | none |
| P02b | `P02b.ab1`: PART R1, R2, R3, every order | primary | expressible | none |
| P02c | `P02c.ab1`: `begin` R1 R2 R3 `end`, one stage | primary | expressible | none |
| P03a | `P03a.ab1`: conc; `conc(ca, cb, c)` | primary | expressible | none |
| P03b | `P03b.ab1`: conc; `conc(a, b, cc)` | primary | expressible | none |
| P03c | `P03c.ab1`: conc; `conc(ca, b, cc)` | primary | expressible | none |
| P03d | `P03d.ab1`: conc; `conc(a, cb, cc)` | primary | expressible | none |
| P03e | `P03e.ab1`: conc, rev; `rev(ra, b)` | primary | expressible | none |
| P03f | `P03f.ab1`: conc, rev; `rev(a, rb)` | primary | expressible | none |

Nothing was judged not expressible, so there are no named variants. Every
program is a transcription: no extra argument, case, key, or reordering.
Expressibility here is the author's judgement; it does not anticipate the
outcome. P03f, for instance, is expected by the problem file to reach the
budget after its one answer in some systems; that is a result, not a
reason to reformulate.

### The definitions

conc (P01, P03), its two cases in the problem's order, case 2's head as
equations and then its condition:

    conc'=lambda p, q, r
        begin {p = [] q = r or
               p = [h'&k'] r = [h&m'] conc(k, q, m)} end

rev (P03e, P03f), likewise, with its two conjuncts in the stated order:

    rev'=lambda p, r
        begin {p = [] r = [] or
               p = [h'&k'] rev(k, n') conc(n, [h], r)} end

- The lambda's parameters stand for the case heads' three (two) places;
  each head pattern is an equation on a parameter, as in Elcock 1990's
  `app`. The names inside differ from the problem's (`p, q, r, h, k, m, n`
  for `a, b, c, h, a, c, q`): in the 1969 notation an unprimed name that a
  lambda does not bind is shared with the whole text, and the problem's
  own names are the sub-problems' top-level unknowns. Renaming is not a
  token class change.
- Local names are introduced with a prime at their first occurrence, once
  each (`docs/decisions.md`, rule 6), as FE69's `map` and `item` do. The
  procedure name is primed where it is defined (`conc'=`, `item'=`).
- P03a–d define only conc, which is all they use; P03e and P03f define
  conc and then rev, the vocabulary's order.

### Idioms and their sources

| idiom | source | used in |
|---|---|---|
| equations as assertions, side by side | Foster and Elcock 1969, "x=y y = 2" (`examples/assertions.ab1`) | P01a, P01c |
| a relation as `name'=lambda x, y begin {A or B} end`, primes for new names | Foster and Elcock 1969, `map` and `item` (`examples/map.ab1`, `examples/triples.ab1`; tutorial ch. 8) | P01b, P03 |
| lists `[a;b]`, `[]`, `[h&t]`; ⟨e1,…,en⟩ ++ x as `[e1;…;en&x]` | Foster and Elcock 1969 (tutorial ch. 8, ch. 10) | P01, P03 |
| the two cases as `{R = [], S = T} or {R = [X|L], T = [X|N], app(L, S, N)}` | Elcock 1990, p. 8 (`examples/append.abs`; tutorial ch. 4) | conc, rev |
| arithmetic as an assertion in any direction | Foster and Elcock 1969, "a = b + 1 … equivalent" (tutorial ch. 8); Foster 1968, pass sets | P02 |
| the relations written `u+v = 16`, `w*u = v`, `u+10 = 12` | Elcock 1982, p. 123 (`examples/relation-list.ab2`) | P02 |
| `begin … end` for one conjunction of assertions | Foster and Elcock 1969 (`docs/decisions.md`, "Three notations") | P02c |

### Constants

Each program's constants are in its block (`% CONSTANTS BEGIN` … `END`),
one per line, written in the 1969 notation, each tagged in a trailing
comment with the stage (or, in P02b, the part) that uses it, and referred
to by name in that stage. Under the harness's replacement (3.9), a constant
reaches the system only with its stage. The names (`zval`, `left`, `sval`,
`pfx`, `r1sum`, `r3add`, `r3sum`, `ca`, `cb`, `cc`, `ra`, `rb`) are used
for nothing else. No program depends on the values: P02's constants are
any integers, P01 and P03's any sequences (with P01a's any value).

## Ambiguities, and the readings taken

1. **P01c's constant is a sequence spliced into a list.** The stage is
   x = ⟨seq⟩ ++ x. In Absys, ⟨e1,…,en⟩ ++ x is the list `[e1;…;en&x]`,
   and there is no ++ to apply to a whole list value. So the block holds
   the sequence's *members* as the 1969 notation writes them inside a
   list, without brackets: `pfx = 1` for ⟨1⟩, and a variant ⟨1,2⟩ would
   be `pfx = 1;2`, giving `x = [1;2&x]`. A variant whose sequence is ⟨⟩
   would need `x = x` instead, which this form cannot give; the verifier
   should know that. The alternative, `conc(pfx, x, x)` with `pfx = [1]`,
   would take any sequence but replaces the problem's equation by an
   application of conc that the problem does not state (R), and was not
   chosen.
2. **P02c, "as one stage, in that order".** In the 1969 notation,
   assertions side by side are accepted one at a time, each elaborated
   before the next (harness README 3.2, decision 17), which would make
   P02c compute exactly as P02a. Elcock's 1982 program is one assertion
   (`… and … and …`), whose three relations go on one list in that order.
   The reading taken: one conjunction, `begin R1 R2 R3 end`, one
   assertion with one budget (harness QUESTIONS A1 says the choice is the
   author's).
3. **The notation for P01 and P03.** The rule picks the earliest notation
   with every construct needed. Whether the 1969 notation's relations
   without `=> z` and `key` are as FE69 wrote them is not shown by the
   extracts; the reconstruction's grammar allows them (tutorial ch. 10),
   and FE69's `map` and `small` are such relations. The 1969 notation was
   taken.

# Questions: the Absys harness

*What the common contract (`harnesses/README.md`, `harnesses/QUESTIONS.md`)
or the specification could not be implemented as written for Absys, or
left open, and the reading implemented here. No frozen file was changed.
An amendment can settle any of them.*

## A1. The budget counts per assertion, not per stage

`PROTOCOL.md`: 10⁶ steps "per stage and per computation". The systems
file's step is "one step of the machine, as its `--steps` budget counts
them", and `--steps N` is "the budget of steps for each assertion"
(`src/main.rs`): `Session::accept` elaborates each assertion for at most N
steps. A stage's section may hold several assertions (a definition and an
application, several facts). The repl offers no way to change the budget
while it runs, and reports no step count, so the harness cannot stop a
stage when its assertions together reach 10⁶.

**Implemented:** `--steps B` with the problem's B, per assertion. A stage is
*budget* when the system reports derivations still elaborating at its end.
A stage of *m* assertions may spend up to *m*·B steps; when a cost run
shows a stage over B without *budget*, the record says so in a note. A
program author who wants the stage's budget to be exactly B can write a
stage as one assertion (a conjunction `{…, …}` in the 1990 notation,
`begin … end` in 1969); that choice is the author's and changes the order
in which the machine takes the parts, so the harness does not require it.

## A2. Behaviour from the baseline, or answers in full

The systems file says results "report the baseline commit for behaviour
and the instrumented commit for store", and also that `--full`, on the
instrumented branch, exists "so `observe()` can read every answer". The
baseline prints at most 32 elements of a list and 24 derivations, and P13
has lists of up to 10⁵ elements. One run cannot do both.

**Implemented:** behaviour runs use `absys-measure` (`5450449`) with
`--full` and without `--measure`. The systems file records that its
default output is identical to the baseline's in 140 runs and `--full`'s
in the 132 the baseline did not cut short; the qualification checks again
that every `print()` the harness records equals the baseline `absys
FILE`'s output, where nothing is cut short. Records say `instrumented:
true` and give the measure commit.

## A3. Where the system's output for a stage ends

The repl prints nothing when it has finished with a line (no prompt when
its input is not a terminal), so the harness cannot tell from its output
alone that a stage is done.

**Implemented:** after each section the harness writes `.help`, a command
of the repl that only prints a fixed text; the text marks the end. If a
section ends inside an unfinished assertion, the repl reads `.help` as its
continuation and replies ``error at L:1: `.` is not in the notation``,
which the harness recognises as the same mark, and records as the stage's
error. `check` rejects such a section, so a checked program never meets
it.

## A4. Steps and store only for a whole text

The repl, the incremental system, reports no step count and no store;
`--measure` (the systems file's qualified measurement) works only in
`absys FILE`, which reads the whole file before it starts and prints its
results at the end. A cost or storage run cannot both receive stage *k*
only when it is posed and measure it.

**Implemented:** each stage *k* of a cost or storage run is a new process,
`absys-measure FILE --measure --full`, FILE the text of the parameters,
prelude and stages 1 to *k*. Its session accepts the assertions one at a
time, like the repl's, so its state and each assertion's steps at stage
*k* are those of the incremental session; the qualification checks this
for every stage of every test. The records say what was done:
`posed.how: "reposed"`, `reason: "configuration"` (the schema has no
reason for "the measurement's way"), the steps of stages 1 to *k*−1 as
`restart_cost` (in-run), `steps.stage` the steps of stage *k*'s own
assertions (the incremental cost) and `steps.restated` the whole run.
Absys's behaviour runs pay no restart cost; classifiers should not read
one from these records. A syntax error anywhere in stages 1 to *k* stops
the whole `absys FILE` run with no output, where the repl would have gone
on: after an error, a cost or storage run measures nothing more.

## A5. spawn() in a system with one computation

P09a, P09b and P16b spawn computations "in the same instance of the
system, sharing one database". Absys has one computation per session: an
assertion is added to every derivation, and there is nothing else to add
it to. The systems file lists no concurrency.

**Implemented:** `spawn(c)` gives the system the computation's SPAWN
subsection, into the one session, after the previous computation has run
"to its end or its budget" (`side_by_side: false`). Each spawned
computation's answers and state are read right after its own section,
before the next is given, since that is the moment it has run to its end;
the next computation's are read with it included. (`PROTOCOL.md` lists
the calls as spawn, then answers; in a configuration that runs one
computation to its end before the next, this reading takes each one's
answers at its end.) Each has its own budget, per assertion as in A1.

Because the spawned computations are one computation, they share every
unknown. So for P16b the harness spawns the four contributors and does not
use `spawn_fallback`; that the fallback ("posed as one conjunction in
main") and Absys's spawn come to the same computation is for the
classifiers to note. Whether P09a's "not conjoined" can be met at all is
the program author's and the classifiers' question, not the harness's.

## A6. A commit stage in a system that never selects

At a commit stage "the system selects one of its current outcomes v", and a
reposed run replays it as x = v. Absys keeps every derivation live, and
has no way to receive v at run time: it reads no input.

**Implemented:** the program's section for a commit stage is given as it
is (it may hold only comments). `answers(1)` is the first derivation
printed, as for any any-one query; it is not a selection, and the record
says so in a note. `replayed_commitments` is always empty, and a reposed
run replays the commit stage's section as written. `validate.py` warns of
this ("the system selected nothing?"), as the contract foresees.

## A7. emit, and when an effect is performed

The contract's emit appends m "rendered as the system renders m". Absys's
one external effect is `tout(label, term)`, which keeps its output in the
derivation that performed it: a derivation that later fails loses its
outputs from the printed state.

**Implemented:** `tout("emit", T)` is the binding of emit. The harness
reads each output from the system's trace (an `output` event, `emit =
VALUE`), at the moment it is performed, so an output of a derivation that
later fails is still in the log. The entry is the text after `emit = `.
The trace is on in P11 runs only (and in cost runs with the 10⁶ budget,
for repeated work); it prints the events the machine records in every
run, and changes nothing.

## A8. alternatives pending

The state means a system "has stopped after an answer, and holds
alternatives that a request for more answers would resume". Absys
elaborates every derivation before it reports, and reports all of them; no
request resumes anything, under fair or depth-first search.

**Implemented:** the harness never records *alternatives pending*. The
derivations held are counted in `alternatives.at_boundary` (unit:
derivation), and those beyond the cap are in `observe.raw`.

## A9. How a program learns its instance's parameters and orders

The contract has the program "take n, an arrival order, a spawn order or
the answer mode from the harness". An Absys program reads no input, and
its stages are fixed text.

**Implemented:** (1) parameters the program declares (`% PARAMETERS`) are
given to the system as assertions `NAME = VALUE`, written by the harness
in the program's notation, before the prelude; (2) where the order names
the stages' relations (P02b, P07a), a program may write them as PART
sections, and the harness gives part `order[k-1]` at stage *k*. Both are
listed as confounds. Without (2), a program would have to choose each
stage's relation from `order` with its own code, adding alternatives and
steps the problem does not have.

## A10. Where the constants are, without anticipation

The constants must be in one place the verifier can replace, and a stage's
constants may not reach the system before that stage (`PROTOCOL.md`,
"Writing a program", rule 5). In Absys every assertion is a relation the
machine holds and acts on, so a block of assertions `c = 7` given at
stage 1 would give the system later stages' constants as information from
stage 1.

**Implemented:** the block, in the prelude, is a table `NAME = VALUE` that
the harness reads and never gives to the system. When it gives a section
(the prelude, a stage, a part, a spawned computation), it replaces each
name of the table in that section's text by its value, textually, outside
quoted constants and comments (README, 3.9). A constant reaches the system
only with the section that uses it. The verifier replaces only the block.
The replacement is listed as a confound; the qualification shows, for
X10a in every mode, that a later stage's constant is not in the system's
state before its stage, and that no constant's name reaches the system.

## A11. check, with no parse-only mode

The brief asks whether `absys lsp` can give diagnostics without running
the text. It cannot: its diagnostics accept each assertion with a budget
of 20 000 steps (`src/lsp.rs`, `analyse`), and report, among others,
"after this assertion no derivation survives".

**Implemented:** `check` uses `absys-measure json FILE --steps 0`, which
parses, compiles and adds each assertion to the goal, and takes no step;
it reads only the error and the count, and it stops if the system reports
a step or an event. Adding an assertion to the goal without a step is not
running it: nothing is elaborated, no binding made, no output performed.

## A12. A reposed stage whose replay cannot finish

Rule 5 of `validate.py`: a reposed stage has a measured restart cost. If
the replay of stages 1 to *k*−1 cannot finish (the system is killed for
lack of memory, or stopped at ten times the safety limit), the restart
cost cannot be measured, and nothing honest can stand in for it.

**Implemented:** `restart_cost: null`, the reason in `harness_faults`, and
the record is kept as `<run_id>.INVALID.json` with exit 3. With enough
memory (README, section 1), the replay of a stage that ended in *budget*
always finishes, since every assertion stops at the budget.

## A13. An error the system recovers from

The repl reports a syntax error and goes on with the next line, so the
session could continue. `PROTOCOL.md` reposes after an error "in every
configuration, incremental ones included".

**Implemented:** the stage is *error*, with the system's message
verbatim (and *suspended* beside it if a derivation holds suspended
work), and the next stage is reposed into a new session, replaying every
section, the erroneous one included.

## A14. Probes

The brief asks for the systems file's probes to be run. `systems/absys/`
has none (only Python and SWI-Prolog have `probes/`).

**Implemented:** the qualification uses its own made-up programs, and the
system's own output run directly as the reference.

# Harnesses: the common contract

*Phase 4 (`PROTOCOL.md`, "Phases"), wave 1, written against `spec-1.0`.
This is the part every per-system harness shares. It changes no frozen
file. Where the specification could not be implemented as written, or was
ambiguous, the reading taken here is in [`QUESTIONS.md`](QUESTIONS.md).*

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| `README.md` | this contract: what every per-system harness implements, and what every program is written against |
| [`stages.json`](stages.json) | the structure of every problem: sub-problems, instances (sizes, orders, answer modes), and per stage its number, description, queries and caps, commit and spawn, and the problem file's line. **No constants, no valid outcomes** |
| [`record.schema.json`](record.schema.json) | the JSON Schema of a raw record, the same for every system |
| [`validate.py`](validate.py) | checks raw records against the schema and the rules below (Python 3, standard library only) |
| [`QUESTIONS.md`](QUESTIONS.md) | what the specification leaves open, and the reading implemented |
| [`examples/`](examples) | **made-up** records and a made-up stages file, written by hand to test `validate.py`. Not runs, not results |
| `<system>/` | one per system, written by that system's harness author: `run`, `check`, its `README.md`, `S-mechanisms.md`, `qualification/` |

Words in this file: *must*, *never* and *only* are requirements; a
per-system harness that cannot meet one says so in its own `QUESTIONS.md`
and README.

## 1. The first principle

**A harness observes what the system computes. It never supplies it.**

A harness passes stages in, collects answers through the system's
standard mechanism for answers, reads state for `observe()`, enforces the
budget and the safety limit, and writes the record. It does not, on the
system's or the program's behalf:

- suspend a computation, or wait for information;
- search, backtrack, or enumerate values;
- schedule, interleave or arbitrate between computations, or run
  computations concurrently itself (`PROTOCOL.md`: concurrency is a
  mechanism of the configuration);
- propagate constraints, or simplify, reconstruct, complete or combine
  answers;
- combine stages, work out the net information of a reposed run, or skip
  a replayed stage;
- order, choose, retry or re-pose goals on its own.

Where a configuration lacks a mechanism, the harness does not make up for
it. The program must, as S code counted against that configuration, or
the problem is *not expressible* there. Everything a harness does beyond
passing stages in, collecting answers and reading state is listed in its
README as a possible confound, and copied into each record's
`run.confounds`.

## 2. Terms

| term | meaning |
|---|---|
| **instance** | one thing a harness runs: a sub-problem at one size, in one arrival or spawn order, in one answer mode. Its id comes from `stages.json` (`P01a`, `P02b.R2R1R3`, `P12c.n16.any`, `P13d.n10000`, `P16a.n1000.interleaved`). A sub-problem with one instance has the sub-problem's own id |
| **run** | one invocation of `harnesses/<system>/run`: one configuration, one instance, one mode, every stage of the instance in order. It writes one raw record |
| **stage** | as the problem file numbers it (`stages.json` gives the line). Stage k's information is held by the program, never by the harness |
| **computation** | `main`, the instance's one computation (or its top level); or a computation started with `spawn()` (P09a, P09b, P16b), named as `stages.json` names it |
| **attempt** | one try at a stage under the safety limit. A stage has one attempt, or two when the first was stopped by the safety limit and the problem allows a rerun |
| **query** | one call of `answers(cap)` on one computation at the end of a stage. Each stage of `stages.json` lists its queries with their caps |

The query of a stage is always about all the information of stages 1 to k
(`SPECIFICATION.md`, "Stages and monotonicity"), over the sub-problem's
unknowns. `stages.json` lists those unknowns by name; their values are
for the classifiers.

## 3. How a run is driven

    harnesses/<system>/run CONFIGURATION PROBLEM SUBPROBLEM MODE PROGRAM OUTDIR

| argument | value |
|---|---|
| CONFIGURATION | a configuration of `systems/<system>/README.md`, by its name there (`absys-depth-first`, `plain`, `core`, `x1sim`, ...) |
| PROBLEM | `P01` … `P16` |
| SUBPROBLEM | an **instance id** from `stages.json`, which for a sub-problem with one instance is the sub-problem id (`P07c`), and otherwise names its parameters (`P12a.n8.all`). See `QUESTIONS.md`, Q2 |
| MODE | `behaviour`, `cost` or `storage` (section 8) |
| PROGRAM | the program's path, relative to the repository root |
| OUTDIR | where the raw record is written: `results/<system>/<configuration>/<problem>/raw/` (section 10) |

Exit status: **0** when a valid record was written, whatever the run's
outcome (an *error*, *budget* or *timeout* stage is a result, not a
failure of the harness); **2** for a usage error (unknown configuration,
instance or mode; a mode the systems file does not allow for that
configuration, such as `cost` for *x1sim*), with no record written;
**3** when the harness itself failed and could not write a valid record.
A harness fault that still allows a record is written into
`harness_faults` and exits 0.

**The harness runs inside that system's pinned Linux image**
(`sandbox/README.md`, `PINS.md`): `cp-systems:spec-1.0` (Absys, ALGOL 60,
x1sim), the pinned `swipl:11.0.1` image, the pinned `python:3.13.7`
image. It assumes nothing of the host. It needs only what the image has,
plus the repository mounted at a path it is given or finds from its own
location. It records the system build it ran (section 9). The launcher
outside the container (whatever starts it) is not part of the harness and
may not change what it does; it may pass the image digest in, by an
environment variable the system harness names, since the harness cannot
always read it from inside.

What `run` does, in this order, and nothing else:

1. Read `harnesses/stages.json`; find the instance; take its stages, its
   queries and caps, its commit and spawn stages, and its limits (a
   problem's `limits`, else `default_limits`).
2. Check the program with nothing but reading its bytes (SHA-256) and,
   where the systems file needs it, the constants input (section 11).
3. For k = 1 … K: **pose** stage k (section 4); for each spawned
   computation of the stage, **spawn** it; for each query of the stage,
   **answers(cap)**; then **observe()** and **print()**; then record the
   attempt. Apply the safety limit (section 7); after a stop, rerun once
   where allowed.
4. Write the record, then validate it with `validate.py`. A record that
   does not validate is a harness fault (exit 3), kept beside the output
   under the name `<run_id>.INVALID.json`, never silently dropped.

`run` never decides, from what a stage returned, to pose a different
stage, to skip one, or to stop early. The only things that change how the
next stage is posed are the ones `PROTOCOL.md` names: *budget*, *error*,
and (`QUESTIONS.md`, Q7) *timeout*. P13's rule that larger n are not run
after a limit stop is applied by whoever runs the batch, across runs, not
by `run` (Q10).

These are `PROTOCOL.md`'s, made concrete. A per-system harness implements
exactly these and nothing that orders, chooses or re-poses goals on its

- **reposed**: a new computation is started, and stages 1 to k are
  replayed into it **in order, every one of them, replacements and
  withdrawals included** (P10, P15d). The program carries them out. The

## 11. What a program must provide

A program author cannot run anything before the program is fixed (only
the system harness's `check`, which executes nothing). So each system
harness's README says exactly, per configuration, how a program meets
these requirements; the common part is:

1. **Stages as units the harness can pose.** The program handles stage k
   when, and only when, the harness poses it, in the way the
   configuration receives stages (incremental, or by replaying 1 … k).
   Code for stage k does not depend on any later stage.
2. **Replay.** In a reposed run the program carries out every stage
   1 … k in order, replacements and withdrawals included, and accepts a
   replayed commit stage as the information x = v, with v as the harness
   passes it (the verbatim answer of the commit stage).
3. **Instance parameters.** The program takes n, an arrival order, a
   spawn order or the answer mode from the harness, as `stages.json`
   names them, and holds everything else.
4. **Answers through the standard mechanism.** Answers reach the harness
   only through the configuration's standard mechanism for answers, in
   the form the system harness's README fixes (for Python and ALGOL 60,
   printed lines with the delimiters it defines).
5. **State for observe().** Whatever the system does not expose by
   itself (a Python program's named pending structure, its counters of
   problem operations), the program exposes in the form the system
   harness reads. Counters that only count are H (`METRICS.md`).
6. **Constants for the verifier** (`PROTOCOL.md`, "Writing a program",
   rule 6). Every constant of every stage is in **one** place the
   verifier can replace without touching anything else, and the program
   stays correct for other constants. Which place is fixed per system by
   its harness README, not here, with this default:

   | system | where the constants are |
   |---|---|

   A sub-problem with no constants (P04d, P04f, P08b; `variants/README.md`)
   records `none`. Sizes n and arrival orders are not constants (they are
   not varied) and come from the harness (point 3).
7. **Provenance** (`PROTOCOL.md`, "Writing a program", rules 1, 2, 8): its
   author, whether the author had seen a precursor, and the source of each
   idiom, in a comment the system harness README places.

**H tokens** (`METRICS.md`, class H) are the per-system harness's own
calls as they appear in a program: the calls that pose stages, request
answers and print, the emit stub's binding, and output adapters (rule
13). Each system harness's README lists them, construct by construct,
before any program is written. Code a program adds beyond them is
classed by the rules of `METRICS.md`, not as H.

As its brief says (`sandbox/briefs/harness-system.md`), under

# What the reconstruction does, and what each rule rests on

Every rule of the machine is listed here with its evidence. Three kinds of
statement are kept apart:

- **Source**: what a primary source says. The page is given. The sources
  are listed in `sources/README.md`.
- **Decision**: what the reconstruction does where the sources are silent,
  ambiguous or in conflict. The reason is given.
- **Experiment**: an option that is not historical. It exists only so the
  rule beside it can be studied.

The abbreviations are:

- **E90**: Elcock, "Absys: the first logic programming language: a
  retrospective and a commentary", *J. Logic Programming* 9 (1990) 1-17.
- **FE69**: Foster and Elcock, "Absys 1: an incremental compiler for
  assertions; an introduction", *Machine Intelligence 4* (1969). Only OCR
  extracts of most of its sections have been seen, not its last pages.
- **F68**: Foster, "Assertions: programs written without specifying
  unnecessary order", *Machine Intelligence 3* (1968).
- **E82**: Elcock, "Goal selection strategies in Horn clause programming",
  *Proc. 4th Biennial CSCSI/SCEIO Conference* (1982) 121-124, read from the page
  scans (`sources/notes/elcock-1982.md`). It was found after the first
  version of this reconstruction, and the rules it changed say so.

## Three notations, one machine

1. **The 1990 notation** (`.abs`) is the one E90 uses. E90 says it takes
   "some slight liberties ... with the original syntax" (p. 3), and calls
   what it describes "a subset of the language Absys-4, circa 1968". The
   source is E90 pp. 3, 8, 11, 15.
   - Procedures are written `name = lambda R, S, T` and a body.
   - `{…}` is a conjunction, with its members separated by commas.
   - `or` gives alternatives.
   - Lists are written `[]`, `[1,2]` and `[X|L]`.
   - Constants are quoted: `'BROWN'`.
   - `not(…)`, `{set(X), {…}, S}` and `tout("U", U)` are available.

2. **The 1969 notation** (`.ab1`) is the notation of Absys 1, as far as the
   FE69 extracts show it. The source is FE69.
   - Assertions are written side by side, with no separator.
   - `begin … end` groups assertions.
   - `{A1 or A2}` gives alternatives.
   - Lists are written `[a;b;c]`, and `[h&t]` for a head and a tail.
   - `x'` introduces a new name.
   - `lambda x, y => z key x begin … end` defines a function with a result
     and a key.
   - `null(p)` and arithmetic `a = b + 1` are available.

   The 1982 notation (`.ab2`) is the one E82 uses for its examples: the
   1969 notation, with `<< … >>` for `{ … }`, `and` written between
   assertions, lists written `[a,b]` and `[h|t]`, and no primes. The source
   is E82 pp. 122-123.

3. *Decision.* **All three notations read into the same tree and run on the
   same machine.** E90 presents its Absys as the language of FE69 with a
   different surface, and E82 draws "heavily on Foster and Elcock (1969)".
   Nothing in the sources suggests that they evaluate differently.

## Terms

4. *Source.* **The only functor is the list constructor**, so the Herbrand
   universe is lists and constants (E90 p. 10). There are no `f(t1, …, tn)`
   terms. E90 suggests writing `[f, t1, …, tn]` instead.

5. *Decision.* **Constants are numbers and quoted words.** In the 1990
   notation `'BROWN'` and `"U"` are both constants. They are equal only to
   themselves, and the two kinds of quote are never equal to each other.
   - E90 p. 15 quotes the student data as `'BROWN'`.
   - E90 note 11 writes the label of `tout` as `"U"`.
   - FE69 and F68 quote constants with `'`, as in `'='` and `'+'`.

6. *Source.* **An identifier is a variable**, and `app = lambda …` is an
   equation that instantiates `app` (E90 p. 8: "The syntax of procedure
   definitions is borrowed from the lambda calculus"). E90 p. 10 says "When
   created, an identifier is associated with ... an uninstantiated
   variable".
   - *Decision.* An application of an identifier that has no value yet
     waits until it has one. E90 says an uninstantiated identifier holds "a
     list of references to suspended processes which ... require the
     identified variable to be instantiated for completion" (p. 10). So a
     procedure can be applied before it is defined.
   - *Decision.* In the 1990 notation:
     - Inside a lambda, a variable written with a capital is *local* when
       it is not bound by the lambda.
     - An identifier written with a small letter is a name the whole text
       shares, such as `app` or `math-course`.
     - Outside any lambda, every identifier is shared by the whole text,
       which is what lets `rev([5],[V])` refer to the `V` of an earlier
       assertion (E90 p. 13).
   - *Source.* In the 1969 notation, the names introduced with a prime are
     local (FE69: "The primes in the above serve to introduce new names").
   - *Decision.* A prime's scope is the whole lambda, not the `begin … end`
     around it. Each name is primed only once in every example.
   - *Decision.* The 1982 notation has no primes. In its `mem`, `p` and
     `sl` are local and `mem` is not. Here, inside a lambda, a name that the
     body uses but never applies, and that the lambda does not bind, is
     local; a name it applies belongs to the whole text.

7. *Source.* **The local variables of an alternative are created when it is
   chosen.** E90 p. 8 calls them existentially quantified.
   - *Decision.* A local variable belongs to the innermost alternative (or
     body of `not` or `set`) that contains every occurrence of it.
   - *Decision.* The variables a derivation creates are numbered with
     subscripts, `X₁, L₁, N₁`, which number increasing each time a
     derivation enters a part of a body that has local variables.
   - Together these reproduce E90's own numbering, including `X₄` and `L₄`
     for the variables of the later assertion `rev([5],[V])` (p. 13).

8. *Source.* **There is no occur check** (E90 p. 11).

## Equality, and suspension

9. *Source.* **Equality is a process taking two references** (E90 pp. 10-11):
   - Two lists: equate their heads and their tails.
   - The same constant, or the same variable: succeed.
   - A list and a constant, or two different constants: fail, which ends
     the derivation.
   - An uninstantiated variable and a term: instantiate the variable, and
     add "any suspended equality processes associated with x ... to the
     goal of the current computation".

10. *Source.* **An equation between two different uninstantiated variables
    is suspended** "and associated with both x and y" (E90 p. 11). It is
    processed again when either variable is instantiated.
    - *Source.* **A primitive relation stays associated with every variable
      it was associated with**, and comes back each time one of them is
      bound, even after it has been elaborated. E82 p. 123 says binding "a
      variable ... automatically returns any relations associated with that
      variable to the list of relations still to be elaborated", and its
      example shows w*2 = 14 on that list twice, and 2+14 = 16 "found
      satisfied" after it was already elaborated. Equations and arithmetic
      behave this way here. Anything else that waits (an application, a
      `not`, `tout`) comes back once. The first version of this
      reconstruction returned every process once. E82 changed it.
    - *Decision, on conflicting evidence.* **A returned relation goes to the
      head of the list.** E82 says the relations "appended", but the lists
      it prints come out only if they go to the head. Appended to the end,
      the list it prints as (2+14 = 16; w*2 = 14; w*2 = 14) would be (w*2 =
      14; 2+14 = 16; w*2 = 14), and its next step, "The first relation is
      examined ... and found satisfied", would be false. The bindings at the
      end are the same either way (`tests/historical.rs`, `e82_p123_*`).
      *Experiment.* `--wake back` appends them. So a derivation
    can finish with suspended equations: its "binding environment exhibits
    a 'partially' solved form constrained by the suspended equations" (p.
    12). `absys` shows these. Asked for `U` after `rev([1,2,U],[V|L])`, it
    says `U = V` and gives the equations `U = X₃` and `X₃ = V` that make it
    so.

11. *Decision.* **One equation is elaborated in one step.** E90 says the
    list case "in effect spawns equality processes between the heads and
    tails". Here they are worked through at once, inside the same step,
    and the processes they wake are added to the goal. Nothing the sources
    show depends on the difference.

12. *Source.* **Equations are elaborated as they arise, before the next
    application.**
    - E90 p. 6: "Absys normally processes 'unification equations' as they
      arise".
    - E90 p. 9: "the ongoing equation solving establishes bindings which
      are immediately used".
    - *Decision.* A derivation therefore keeps two queues. It always takes
      an equation first if it has one, and otherwise a literal.

## Alternatives, and the search

13. *Source.* **`or` distributes through the goal of the derivation it is
    in.** E90 p. 9: it is "essentially creating two new goals which can
    notionally be regarded as initiating parallel derivations". FE69:
    "Unsatisfiable conjunctions disappear when unsatisfiability is
    detected", and, a few sentences later, the conjunctions "in effect
    constitute parallel non-interacting programs".
    - Each alternative gets a copy of the derivation: its bindings, its
      suspended processes and the rest of its goal.
    - *Decision.* The copy is made when the `or` is reached, which for an
      application is the step after the application. FE69 says Absys 1
      shared processing between the copies ("in a way which attempts to
      minimise unnecessary duplication"). That changes cost, not results.

14. *Source.* **The search is fair.** E90 p. 10: "the implementation of
    Absys used a 'fair' search rule, in that all derivations continue to be
    incrementally elaborated until found unsatisfiable". The derivations
    take a step each, in turn.
    - *Experiment.* `--search depth-first` elaborates the first derivation
      until it fails or hibernates, as a backtracking Prolog would.
    - Kowalski (1988) credits Absys with "the central role of
      backtracking", and E82 p. 122 says: "each conjunction notionally
      constituting a separate (parallel) computation branch ... In practice,
      of course, the non-determinism was handled by appropriate differential
      record keeping and backtracking in a similar spirit to Prolog
      implementations." So the designer's own accounts disagree: in 1982
      the implementation backtracked; in 1990 it "used a 'fair' search
      rule". Backtracking and fairness are compatible only if the
      backtracking interleaved the branches, which E82 does not say. One
      reading reconciles them: "differential record keeping" is how a
      branch's state was kept and restored (a trail), which says nothing
      about the order in which branches were taken up. That reading is
      ours; neither paper states it.
    - *Decision, on conflicting evidence.* The derivations here are
      elaborated fairly, as E90 says, which is also the "notional" meaning
      E82 gives. `--search depth-first` is the backtracking reading. Nothing
      published gives a result that tells the two apart.

15. *Decision, on conflicting evidence.* **Within a derivation, the body of
    an application takes the place of the literal applied.** So its
    literals are elaborated before the literals that came after it.
    - E90 p. 9 says the goal literal is "replaced by" the body.
    - E90 p. 3 also says "Absys used a fair computation rule", and note 9
      says "Absys does not guarantee a particular order of processing of
      conjuncts".
    - A fair rule, in the sense E90 cites (Lassez and Maher), is one that
      selects every literal eventually. Taking literals strictly in turn
      (first in, first out) is one such rule, not the only one.
    - E90 prints `setdiff` (p. 15) as a definition only, with no query and
      no result, and does not define `mem`. Run on inputs chosen here,
      `[1,2,3,4]` and `[2,4,6]`, with `mem` defined here, strictly in turn
      it computes `[1]`, not `[1,3]`. The reason is that `not`, which is not
      safe (rule 18), is then elaborated before the recursion that
      instantiates its variable.
    - Strictly in turn but with `not` delayed until its variables are
      instantiated, it computes `[1,3]` too. E90 p. 3 mentions "primitive
      and user declared delay constructs" it does not describe.
    - So the example favours the body in the literal's place without
      proving it. The default follows it, as the simplest rule under which
      E90's examples work without an undescribed delay.
    - *Experiment.* `--select fifo` gives the strictly fair literal rule
      (docs/research.md, E02).

16. *Source.* **A derivation with nothing left to do hibernates**, and a
    later assertion can wake it. E90 note 13: "'Hibernate' is a better
    word, since the computational process associated with the derivation
    can be reactivated". It counts as a refutation (p. 11).

17. *Source.* **The system is incremental.**
    - FE69: "as assertions are accepted by the system, whatever processing
      can be done on the basis of data already present in the system is
      done".
    - E90 p. 13 says an assertion typed later is added to the text "and
      augment[s] the goal".
    - *Decision.* Each assertion of a file is accepted in turn. It is added
      to every derivation alive, and the computation runs until each
      derivation hibernates or fails, or the budget runs out (100000 steps
      for each assertion by default).

## Negation and aggregation (1990 notation)

18. *Source.* **`not` starts an independent computation with the criteria
    reversed** (E90 p. 14: it "acts like a degenerate or in that during
    goal evaluation it initiates an independent computational branch, but
    one in which the satisfiability criteria for termination are
    reversed"). If any derivation of the negated assertions reaches a
    refutation, the `not` fails. If every one fails, it holds.
    - *Source.* It is not safe. E90 note 18: "both Absys and PROLOG have
      the shortcoming that they do not use a safe computation rule".
    - *Decision.* The computation starts from the bindings as they stand,
      and does not wait for its variables.
    - *Experiment.* `--negation delayed` makes `not` wait until every
      variable of the negated assertions is instantiated.
    - *Decision.* A derivation of the independent computation that
      hibernates counts as a refutation only if what it leaves suspended is
      equations between variables, or output.
      - E90 counts a derivation that ends with suspended equations as a
        refutation because "the constraint is always satisfiable" (p. 12).
        A process waiting for something else has no such guarantee. An
        example is an application of a procedure not yet defined.
      - If the computation can go no further and has neither a refutation
        nor a failure in every derivation, the `not` is set aside. It waits
        on whatever its computation waited for outside itself, and starts
        again from the bindings as they then stand. That can include an
        identifier of the text it met first, such as a procedure defined
        later.
      - Without this, a `not` or `set` applied before a procedure it uses
        was defined gives a wrong answer (docs/research.md, E02).

19. *Source.* **`{set(X), {…}, S}`** is "the Absys primitive aggregation
    operator set" of Absys-4 (E90 p. 15). The form is transcribed as
    printed.
    - *Decision.* It starts an independent computation, as `not` does.
      When every derivation of it has hibernated or failed, S is equated
      with the list of the distinct values of X in the derivations that
      hibernated, in the order those derivations stand.
    - *Decision.* An empty set gives `[]`, which `setdiff` needs.
    - *Decision.* It counts refutations as `not` does, and waits in the
      same way when it cannot yet be decided.
    - E90 says only that set was "implemented in an analogous way to the
      PROLOG operator". Prolog's `setof` sorts its answers and fails when
      there are none. Neither of those is done here.

20. *Decision.* **`tout("U", U)` writes `U = [2]` when U is complete.**
    E90 note 11 says only that the example refutation "would cause the
    output 'assertion' tout("U", U) to produce 'U = [2]'". It is not said
    when. U is complete only at the end of that refutation, so here `tout`
    waits, like any other process, until its term has no uninstantiated
    variable in it.

## The 1969 notation

21. *Source.* **`key`** (FE69): "The key statement indicates the data that
    must be present before evaluation of the function may take place". An
    application waits until its key variables are instantiated.
    - E90 p. 3 mentions "both primitive and user declared delay
      constructs". `key` is the only user-declared one with a known
      syntax.
    - FE69 says that without `key`, "processing of map might give rise to
      further processing of map ... before processing the assertion p =
      [r'&s']", so that it would not terminate.
      - When the list is already present, that cannot happen under rule
        12, so here `map` without `key` terminates. This is a place where
        the reconstruction is more orderly than Absys 1 promised to be.
      - When the list is not yet present, `map` without `key` goes on for
        ever here, making lists of every length. With `key` it waits.

22. *Source.* **`=> z`**: a function with a result. FE69 says `f(m,n) = b`
    "is equivalent to" the body with `b` for `z`. So `i = item(q)` is the
    application `item(q, i)`. An application inside a term gets a new
    variable for its result.

23. *Source.* **Arithmetic is an assertion, usable in every direction.**
    - FE69: "the assertions a = b + 1, a = 1 + b, 1 + b = a, b + 1 = a are
      equivalent".
    - F68 gives the "pass sets" of `plus(p,q,r)`: any two of the three, or
      all three.
    - `a + b = c` is therefore elaborated when two of a, b and c are
      numbers, and otherwise waits. `-` and `/` are the same relations read
      the other way.
    - *Decision.* Numbers are integers. A division must come out whole.
    - *Decision.* Arithmetic is in the 1969 notation only. E90 shows none,
      and allows `-` in names such as `math-course`.

24. *Decision.* **`null(p)` is `p = []`.**

## What is not reconstructed

- **The higher-order features** of the full Absys-4 language (E90 p. 3,
  described in a report not seen). This includes partial application
  (FE69: "Functions may be introduced by partial application of other
  functions"). A lambda expression inside a lambda expression is refused.
- **The "simple control mechanisms"** of Absys-4 (E90 p. 3), and any
  primitive delay other than the ones above. Their form is unknown.
- **The cost and ordering hints of F68** ("a number may be associated with
  an assertion to indicate the cost of attempting it"). F68 is a design
  paper; it describes the system as then "partly implemented on an Elliott
  4120", and nothing later shows these hints in Absys.
- **The Elliott 4120 implementation itself.** It was written in machine
  code (Reid 2011 quotes Gray on its "tie-in to a manufacturers' machine
  code"), and no listing of it is known to us. This is a
  reconstruction of the language as described, not an emulation of the
  program.

## Defects found in the reconstruction

Faults of this program, not decisions about Absys. Each is fixed in a
commit of its own, and the commit before it is kept as the reference for
everything else it does.

1. **Printing a list that contains itself overflowed the stack.**
   *Found* 2026-11-27, while qualifying measurement for the
   computational-paradigms study, whose problem P01c poses `x = [x]`.
   *In* every commit up to and including 7bb61e6.
   - There is no occur check (decision on equality above), so `x = [x]`
     succeeds and binds x to a list whose element is x. The machine
     computed this correctly. The printer then expanded the element for
     ever, and the run ended with "stack overflow" after the computation
     had finished, before its answer was shown.
   - A cycle through a list's tail (`x = [1|x]`) never had the fault: the
     printer cuts any list after 32 elements.
   - *Fix.* Only the printer changes. A list element that is one of the
     list cells being printed around it is printed as `↻`, so `x = [x]`
     prints `[↻]` and `x = [1, x]` prints `[1,↻]`. Tail cycles print as
     before. `tests/cyclic.rs` covers both kinds of cycle, cycles through
     several variables and into the middle of a list, and shared terms
     that are not cyclic.
   - *Check.* Against 7bb61e6, every example and research text, in eight
     output modes and as JSON, prints byte for byte the same (160 runs).
     Only runs that crashed before print differently.

# absys

Absys, the assertional language J. M. Foster and E. W. Elcock built at the
University of Aberdeen around 1967, reconstructed from what its designers
published about it.

An Absys text is a conjunction of assertions, not a sequence of
instructions. As each assertion is accepted, whatever can be done is done:

- An equation between two unknowns is **suspended** until one of them is
  known.
- A procedure is a relation, used in whichever direction the data allow.
- An `or` splits the computation into **derivations** that are all
  elaborated, fairly, until each fails or **hibernates**. A hibernating
  derivation wakes when a later assertion gives it something to do.

```
$ absys examples/reverse.abs --each --env
…
» rev([1,2,U], [V|L])
  1 derivation:
    derivation #7 (hibernating)
      procedures  rev1, rev
      U = V   (suspended: U = X₃, X₃ = V)
      V = U   (suspended: U = X₃, X₃ = V)
      L = [2,1]
      suspended   U = X₃;  X₃ = V
      environment L/[2,1], X₁/1, L₁/[2,U], X₂/2, L₂/[U], L₃/[]

» rev([5], [V])
  1 derivation:
    derivation #11 (hibernating)
      procedures  rev1, rev
      U = 5
      V = 5
      L = [2,1]
      environment U/5, V/5, L/[2,1], X₁/1, L₁/[2,5], X₂/2, L₂/[5], X₃/5, L₃/[], X₄/5, L₄/[]
```

Those are Elcock's own binding environments (*J. Logic Programming* 9, 1990,
pp. 12-13), variable for variable.

## Status

- **The sources.** No Absys program text, listing or manual from Aberdeen is
  known to us. The reconstruction rests on:
  - Elcock's 1990 retrospective, read in full from the page scans;
  - Elcock's 1982 conference paper comparing Absys with Prolog, which walks
    through Absys's list of relations step by step;
  - Foster's 1968 *Assertions* paper, read in full;
  - OCR extracts of most of the sections of Foster and Elcock's 1969
    introduction to Absys 1.

  See [`sources/README.md`](sources/README.md).
- **Every rule of the machine is listed with its evidence** in
  [`docs/decisions.md`](docs/decisions.md). Each is marked as one of three
  kinds:
  - what a source says, with its page;
  - a decision, where the sources are silent or conflict, with the reason;
  - an experiment, which is not historical.
- **Every computation the sources give a result for comes out as they
  say.** There are 17 acceptance tests, each naming its page
  ([`tests/historical.rs`](tests/historical.rs)). They include every list of
  relations awaiting elaboration that Elcock printed in 1982.
- **Three notations run on the one machine:**
  - the retrospective's (`.abs`), which Elcock says takes liberties with
    the original;
  - the 1969 notation of Absys 1 (`.ab1`), as far as the extracts show it;
  - the 1982 paper's (`.ab2`), with `<< … >>` and `and`.
- **Not reconstructed.** The higher-order features and "simple control
  mechanisms" of Absys-4 are described only in a report not seen, so they
  are not reconstructed.
- **Not yet checked.** Nothing has been checked by a person against the
  sources. No literature search beyond the sources listed has been made, so
  nothing here is claimed as new.

## What reconstructing it found

- **Absys does not unify two unknowns. It waits.**
  - `app([1,2], S, T)` ends with `T = [1,2|N₂]`, and the equation `S = N₂`
    suspended. Asked for U after the reverse example, the system says `U =
    V`, by the suspended `U = X₃` and `X₃ = V`.
  - This is Elcock's "partially solved form", and it is the ordinary result
    of a computation here, not a corner case.
- **The order of the assertions does not change what a text computes,
  except through `not`.**
  - The seven assertions of `research/e03-incremental.abs` were accepted in
    all 5040 orders, and gave one outcome. That held although the procedure
    `rev` is applied before it is defined in many of the orders, and 1260 of
    the orders run out of budget on some assertion before a later one
    bounds it.
  - The cost does change with the order: the same three answers of `app`
    cost 25 steps or 22868.
  - `not(X = 1)` then `X = 2` has no derivation; the other order has `X = 2`.
    That is Elcock's "Absys and PROLOG … do not use a safe computation
    rule".
- **Elcock's own `setdiff` favours one answer to how a derivation chose its
  next literal.** The paper prints only its definition; the inputs and the
  definition of `mem` used here are ours.
  - Taking literals strictly in turn, which is a "fair computation rule",
    computes `[1]` for the difference of `[1,2,3,4]` and `[2,4,6]`.
    `not(mem(X, S2))` is then decided before the recursion has instantiated
    X.
  - Putting an applied body in the place of its literal, which is what the
    paper's "replaced by" says, computes `[1,3]`.
  - Taking literals strictly in turn with `not` delayed until its
    variables are instantiated also computes `[1,3]`, and Elcock mentions
    delays he does not describe. So the example favours the body in the
    literal's place without proving it (`docs/decisions.md`, rule 15).
- **Elcock's 1982 walk-through fixes how relations come back.** A relation
  goes back on the list once for each of its variables that is bound, even
  after it has run, and goes to the head of the list. The paper says
  "appended", but its printed lists come out only if they go to the head.
  The same paper says the alternatives were implemented by "backtracking in
  a similar spirit to Prolog"; the 1990 one says the search was fair
  (`docs/research.md`, E06).
- **Data-directed elaboration stops at the first system that needs
  elimination**, as Elcock said in 1982: x + y = 10 and x - y = 4 leave both
  relations waiting (E09).
- **Run on SWI-Prolog, the same programs give the same answers where both
  answer (E07).** Prolog's left-to-right rule loses three:
  - an endless first alternative;
  - left recursion over a known list;
  - Elcock's arithmetic in his own order.

  Absys gets all three. Coroutines on Foster's pass sets (`when/2`) and
  CLP(FD) recover them in modern Prolog. Only CLP(Q), which treats the
  equations as one system, solves x + y = 10, x - y = 4.
- **The incremental session can be rebuilt in modern Prolog, but not
  without building it** (E07). A SWI-Prolog engine fed one assertion at a
  time keeps bindings, choice points and waiting coroutines between them,
  and reproduces E03 and Elcock's 1982 relations posted one by one. A
  procedure applied before it is defined still needs a layer of its own to
  wait instead of raising an error.
- **Fair search finds what depth-first search never reaches.**
  `{loop(A)} or {A = 1}` gives `A = 1` while the loop runs on. Left
  recursion over known data terminates under either search, because
  equations are elaborated as they arise.
- **Two misprints in the retrospective's example programs**:
  - `C - 'C101'` for `C = 'C101'`;
  - `maths-course` applied where `math-course` is defined.

  Transcribed literally, the second would leave Clark's query waiting for a
  procedure that is never defined. See
  [`sources/notes/elcock-1990.md`](sources/notes/elcock-1990.md).

The experiments, with their numbers, are in
[`docs/research.md`](docs/research.md) (ABSYS-E01 to E07, and E09).

## Install and use

You need [Rust](https://rustup.rs). There are no dependencies.

```bash
cargo install --path .
absys examples/append.abs           # every derivation left at the end
absys examples/reverse.abs --each   # the state after each assertion
absys examples/append.abs --trace   # every step
absys examples/append.abs --env     # whole binding environments, as Elcock writes them
absys repl                          # the incremental system at the keyboard
absys permute FILE                  # accept the assertions in every order
absys graph FILE | dot -Tsvg        # the derivation tree and the suspended processes
absys decisions                     # the rules of the machine, and what each rests on
absys verify                        # every example against its .out
cargo test                          # the acceptance tests, the examples, the tutorial
```

Options, for experiments, not history:

- `--search depth-first`
- `--select fifo`
- `--negation delayed`
- `--steps N`

## A text

```
% Elcock 1990, p. 8
app = lambda R, S, T
    {R = [], S = T} or
    {R = [X|L], T = [X|N], app(L, S, N)}

app(R, S, [1,2])          % three derivations: the three ways of splitting [1,2]
```

The same thing in the 1969 notation looks quite different. Here is Foster
and Elcock's own example:

```
item'=lambda x=>z key x
    begin x = [p'&q'] {z=p or z=item(q)} end
p1 = [1;2;5;6]   p2 = [3;7;1]   p3 = [10;2;7;4]
r'=item(p1)   s'=item(p2)   t'=item(p3)   r+s=t
```

It leaves three derivations: r, s, t are 1, 3, 4; 1, 1, 2; and 6, 1, 7. Those
are the paper's three, in its order.

## In this repository

- [`tutorial/`](tutorial): the language, in ten chapters. Every example in
  it is run by `cargo test`.
- [`examples/`](examples): every program the sources give, each with its
  `.out`.
- [`research/`](research): the texts of the experiments.
- [`web/`](web): the playground.
  - `node web/build.mjs` builds it.
  - Serve `web/` and open `index.html`.
  - For any text it shows: each assertion; the derivations after it, with
    their bindings, suspended equations and waiting processes; the tree of
    alternatives; and every step.
  - `node web/test.mjs` checks the WebAssembly build against the native
    one, and `node web/browser-test.mjs` drives the page in headless
    Chrome.
- [`editors/`](editors): `absys lsp`, a language server, and a Visual Studio
  Code extension with a grammar and a run button.

## Licence

Apache-2.0. The papers belong to their publishers and are not included.
